title: Kamala
focus: entering the city and learning love

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha dreams of Govinda becoming a woman, crosses a river with a kind ferryman who predicts his return, and reaches a city where he sees the beautiful courtesan Kamala. She tells him he needs fine clothes, shoes and money; he learns quickly and, through her, gains a position with the merchant Kamaswami. Kamala becomes his teacher in love.

items.prompt: Evaluate this claim about the chapter: “The ferryman's words at the river foreshadow that Siddhartha's journey into the world is a detour that will lead back.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive in part. “This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back” (Kamala, paragraph 11) supports it: the ferryman names the river as his teacher and predicts Siddhartha's return long before it happens. A fair verdict is that the claim holds as foreshadowing of the plot but misses the chapter's own view, in which the city is a lesson Siddhartha means to learn rather than a detour.

Foreshadowing: The ferryman's parting words ("everything is coming back! You too, Samana, will come back") predict the whole second half of the novel. Dialogue: With Kamala, Siddhartha bargains like a merchant: he has nothing to offer but his three skills, "I can think. I can wait. I can fast." Watch for the river and the ferry: the river he crosses here separates the life of the spirit from the life of the city; he will cross it back.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I can think. I can wait. I can fast” slowly and put it in my own words: Siddhartha tells Kamala his only skills are that he can think, he can wait and he can fast. Next, craft. I notice three short sentences with the same pattern, "I can...," like a confident list of possessions. The strongest word is “fast”: going without food was a beggar's discipline, and he presents it as wealth. Then, effect. What does Siddhartha offer Kamala when he has no money? My answer: With no money, Siddhartha offers Kamala what he can do: think, wait and fast, the patience and self-control of a Samana; these inner powers win him Kamala and Kamaswami's business.

items.text: Who ferries Siddhartha across the river?
items.lookFor: The ferryman
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The ferryman in whose hut he slept. “When the day began, Siddhartha asked his host, the ferryman, to get him across the river.” (Kamala, paragraph 5)

items.text: Whom does the ferryman remind Siddhartha of as they part?
items.lookFor: Govinda
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “‘He is like Govinda,’ he thought with a smile” (Kamala, paragraph 12).

items.text: Where does Siddhartha go on the day after his first visit to Kamala?
items.lookFor: To Kamala’s house in the city
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “He had already discovered Kamala’s house in the city long before, there he turned up the following day.” (Kamala, paragraph 64)

items.text: What three skills does Siddhartha name?
items.lookFor: Thinking, waiting and fasting
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Thinking, waiting and fasting: “I can think. I can wait. I can fast.” (Kamala, paragraph 42) (Kamala’s own list in paragraph 53 adds poetry; paragraph 42 is the line that answers the question.)

items.text: Who gives Siddhartha work?
items.lookFor: The merchant Kamaswami
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Kamaswami, a rich merchant, through Kamala’s help: “They are expecting you at Kamaswami’s, he is the richest merchant of the city.” (Kamala, paragraph 65)

items.text: Retell the three most important events of “Kamala” in order, in one sentence each.
items.lookFor: Siddhartha dreams of Govinda becoming a woman, crosses a river with a kind ferryman who predicts his return, and reaches a city where he sees the beautiful courtesan Kamala. She tells him he needs fine clothes, shoes and money; he learns quickly and, through her, gains a position with the merchant Kamaswami. Kamala becomes his teacher in love.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The ferryman carries him across and predicts his return (Kamala, paragraphs 5–11); he sees Kamala and asks her to teach him love (paragraphs 16–29); she sends him to the merchant Kamaswami (paragraph 65).

items.text: Which characters appear or are mentioned in “Kamala”? Name two and one thing each says or does.
items.lookFor: Names and actions taken from the chapter; check against the teacher summary.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Two of: the ferryman, who asks nothing but friendship (“Commemorate me when you make offerings to the gods” (Kamala, paragraph 11)); Kamala, who laughs and then advises him (paragraphs 30, 41); the young village woman he turns down (paragraph 14).

items.text: Where and when does “Kamala” take place? Point to the line that tells you.
items.lookFor: A place/time detail quoted from the chapter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: By a river, a village and a large city, over a few days. “On this day, he reached the large city before the evening” (Kamala, paragraph 15).

items.text: Reread: “In their midst, carried by four servants in an ornamental sedan-chair, sat a woman, the mistress, on red pillows under a colourful canopy.” What does “ornamental” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: ornamental: decorated; made to look beautiful.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Ornamental” here means: decorated; made to look beautiful. In Kamala, paragraph 16, Siddhartha sees a rich woman carried past in a decorated chair, which is his first sight of Kamala.

items.text: Reread: “Who wouldn’t like to give advice to a poor, ignorant Samana, who is coming from the jackals of the forest?” What does “ignorant” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: ignorant: lacking knowledge.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Ignorant” here means: lacking knowledge. In Kamala, paragraph 39, Siddhartha jokingly calls himself a poor, untaught Samana from the forest as he asks Kamala to advise him.

items.text: What does “Kamala” suggest about entering the city and learning love? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that the city teaches through the senses what teachers could not) backed by one located line, such as the one in Kamala, paragraph 29.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests that the city teaches through the senses what teachers could not. Support: “I would like to ask you to be my friend and teacher, for I know nothing yet of that art which you have mastered in the highest degree” (Kamala, paragraph 29).

items.text: Find one example of characterization in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Kamala is characterized by her laughter at his request (“At this, Kamala laughed aloud.” (Kamala, paragraph 30)): it shows, better than any statement, how absurd a ragged Samana looks in her world.

items.text: How does the symbolism in this chapter shape what we understand about entering the city and learning love?
items.lookFor: Look for objects, places or actions that stand for larger ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The river he crosses stands for the line between the spiritual life and the city; the ferryman’s words make it a teacher (Kamala, paragraph 11). Kamala’s grove and the clothes she demands (paragraph 33) stand for the world of the senses he is entering.

items.text: In the passage that begins “‘I thank you, my benefactor,’”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In Kamala, paragraph 8, “benefactor” is formal and grateful, and “disembarking” makes the step onto the far bank a real arrival; together they mark a polite ascetic crossing into a new world with nothing to pay.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Kamala”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Siddhartha dreams of Govinda becoming a woman, crosses a river with a kind ferryman who predicts his return, and reaches a city where he sees the beautiful courtesan Kamala. She tells him he needs fine clothes, shoes and money; he learns quickly and, through her, gains a position with…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The turn is seeing Kamala (“Siddhartha saw how beautiful she was, and his heart rejoiced.” (Kamala, paragraph 17)). Effect: he decides to learn love and money, which leads him to Kamaswami and the life of the city.

items.text: How does “Kamala” build on “Awakening”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: “Awakening” turns him toward the beauty of the world; here he acts on it, “Siddhartha learned something new on every step of his path, for the world was transformed, and his heart was enchanted.” (Kamala, paragraph 1)

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha claims he simply wants a teacher, but his pride shows when he gives away his rice cake rather than beg (“Suddenly, pride flared up in him.” (Kamala, paragraph 62)); Kamala claims to be practical, yet she helps him freely (Kamala, paragraph 67).

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “Siddhartha says he can think, wait and fast. Why are these powerful skills?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should explain his own reason in Kamala, paragraph 68 onward: the skills let him wait for what he wants without being driven by need, which is why he can bargain with Kamala and later with Kamaswami.

items.text: Where does setting appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with love and attachment?
items.lookFor: Look for where and when events happen and how place shapes action or feeling.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Setting carries the move from spirit to senses: the river crossing (Kamala, paragraph 5), the village woman by the stream (paragraph 14) and the grove (paragraph 16) are each a step toward attachment.

items.text: Background: Courtesans in ancient India could be educated, wealthy and respected. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing courtesans could be educated and respected makes Kamala a real teacher, not a scandal: she bargains, advises and opens doors for him (“I’m opening one door after another for you.” (Kamala, paragraph 67)).

items.text: A critic might argue: “The ferryman's prophecy and the river crossing foreshadow the novel's final setting.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Students can agree that the prophecy points to a return (Kamala, paragraph 11), but the chapter itself only promises “You too, Samana, will come back”; claims about the novel’s ending go beyond this chapter. A text counterpoint: Siddhartha is amused and doubtful (paragraph 10).

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With generosity as the standard, the ferryman acts most wisely (paragraph 9); Siddhartha least when pride makes him throw away food (paragraph 62). Students may instead praise Kamala’s honesty (paragraph 41).

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “Kamala” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about entering the city and learning love?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Kamala’s view of their first talk (Kamala, paragraphs 24–33) works well: it shows her amusement and curiosity and hides the seriousness of his search.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “Kamala”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘Who carries him across the river?’ (the ferryman, paragraph 5); why/how, ‘Why does Kamala help him?’ (paragraphs 67–69); what if, ‘Should he have taken the village woman’s offer?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to the search for self-knowledge: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong but indirect: he says his skills will help him reach any goal (Kamala, paragraph 72, the rock that sinks to the bottom), yet he is now learning from others again. Hesse would need to show what the senses teach him about himself.

items.text: Is the characterization in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective: Kamala and Siddhartha are drawn through bargaining dialogue (paragraphs 24–57). Some readers will find the instant success heavy-handed (paragraphs 64–67).

items.text: Compare how “Kamala” treats entering the city and learning love with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a newcomer learning a world of money or romance and quote Siddhartha’s request (paragraph 29); his twist is that he treats love as an art to be learned.

items.text: Predict what “With the Childlike People” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: Kamala says he needs clothes, shoes and money (paragraph 33) and sends him to Kamaswami (paragraph 65). Prediction: he will become a merchant and a lover while trying to stay a Samana inside.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about entering the city and learning love?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a disciplined outsider entering a glamorous city and asking an expert to teach him. What must stay is the bargain of the three skills (paragraph 42).

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Why does Siddhartha choose Kamala as a teacher after refusing the Buddha?’ The text suggests he wants to learn by experience what words could not give (Kamala, paragraph 29).
